extracted.intended_audience: students preparing for mathematical olympiads; advanced high-school and undergraduate problem solvers
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and problem-solving standards for Olympiad-style algebra, trigonometry, inequalities, sequences, systems, and elementary complex/linear-algebra arguments. The page presents methods to transform, telescope, substitute, factor, and bound expressions to produce short elegant solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telescopic principle (trigonometric sums)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use trigonometric identities to write a sum in the form ∑_{k=2}^n [F(k) − F(k − 1)] so intermediate terms cancel and the sum reduces to F(n) − F(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: multiply ∑_{k=1}^n cos kx by 2 sin x and use product-to-sum identities to obtain a telescoping expression; the section gives worked computations leading to (sin((n+1)x/2)/ (2 sin(x/2))) − 1/2 and notes special-case x = 2mπ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use product-to-sum and product identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Convert products of sine and cosine (or similar products) into sums (or vice versa) to enable telescoping or simplification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied when multiplying a sum by 2 sin x to use sin·cos product-to-sum. Also used in telescopic products examples (e.g., ∏ cos(x/2^n) = sin x / x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arctangent (tan^{-1}) subtraction telescoping
rubrics_metrics.description: Use tan(a − b) or arctangent subtraction formula tan^{-1}u − tan^{-1}v = tan^{-1}((u − v)/(1 + uv)) to rewrite sums of arctangents as telescoping differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: with ak = tan^{-1}k, tan(ak+1 − ak) = 1/(k^2 + k + 1), so ∑ tan^{-1}(1/(k^2+k+1)) telescopes to tan^{-1}(n+1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Check and exclude vanishing denominators
rubrics_metrics.description: When expressions contain denominators that can vanish, the solver must consider only the cases where denominators are nonzero (or treat the singular cases separately).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly warns: 'In the expressions containing denominators that can vanish, consider only the cases where this does not happen.' Examples include trig denominators like sin x, cos x, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telescopic principle for products
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a product as a telescoping product of fractions whose numerators and denominators cancel alternately to reduce the product to a simple factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ∏_{n=2}^(1 − 1/n^2) = 1/2 by expressing each factor as (1+1/n)/(1−1/n) or as (n−1)/n·(n+1)/n and canceling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trigonometric substitution heuristic
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a trigonometric substitution suggested by the algebraic form (e.g., expressions reminiscent of multiple-angle formulas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: x^3 − 3x suggests x = 2 cos u (triple-angle for cosine). Recurrence forms may suggest tangent substitutions (x_n = tan t), and the substitution is usually chosen to simplify structure using known trig identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple-angle identities to reduce polynomial systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate polynomial relations into equalities of cosines/sines at multiple angles to obtain angle congruences and then enumerate solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: mapping x=2 cos u transforms x^3−3x structure into cos 3u relationships, leading to equalities like cos 27u = cos u and a counting argument (degree bound) to list all solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Map recurrences to shifted-angle tangent to show periodicity
rubrics_metrics.description: When a recurrence can be rewritten as a tangent-of-difference, substitute x_n = tan(t − (n−1)θ) to exhibit periodicity from tangent's period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: recurrence xn+1 = (√3 x_n − 1)/(x_n + √3) rewrites as tan(t−π/6) and shows x_{n+6} = x_n, giving period 6.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete the square / nonnegativity of squares
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit x^2 ≥ 0 and complete-the-square manipulations to obtain inequalities and equality cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: rewrite 4x − x^4 ≤ 3 as (x^2 − 1)^2 + 2(x − 1)^2 ≥ 0; also used in multiple inequality problems and in quick Olympiad-style deductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endpoint method: treat expression as linear/convex in each variable
rubrics_metrics.description: View the target expression as a linear or convex function in one variable at a time; maxima/minima over intervals occur at endpoints (for linear functions) or on the boundary (for convex functions) enabling reduction to endpoint values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: For fixed other variables, functions f(x)=|x−a| are convex hence maximized at endpoints; used to deduce that the maximum of ∑_{i<j}|x_i−x_j| occurs when each x_i is 0 or 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationalize denominators to obtain telescoping radical sums
rubrics_metrics.description: Rationalize terms containing square roots to write them as differences of simpler terms, leading to telescoping cancellation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: √(1/(k) + 1/(k+1)) manipulation yields terms like 1/√k − 1/√(k+1), so the sum telescopes to 1 − 1/√(n+1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use AM-GM (Arithmetic Mean–Geometric Mean) to bound quantities and deduce equality
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply AM-GM to derive lower/upper bounds that lead to simple algebraic constraints; check equality cases to pinpoint solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In system a+b+c+d=12 and abcd = 27 + sum(ab...), apply AM-GM to derive abcd ≥ 27 + 6√(abcd), factor and deduce abcd ≥ 9 and hence equality occurs only at a=b=c=d=3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sophie Germain identity and its variants for factorization
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the identity X^4 + 4Y^4 = (X^2 + 2XY + 2Y^2)(X^2 − 2XY + 2Y^2) (and variants) to factor quartic expressions and simplify sums/products or prove compositeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to evaluate sums like ∑ 4k/(4k^4 + 1) and in proofs about representability/compositeness of expressions like n^4 + 4n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nilpotent-matrix inversion via polynomial/exponential identities
rubrics_metrics.description: For matrices with A^m = 0 (nilpotent), find inverses of polynomial expressions in A by algebraic factorization or by truncating the exponential series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: If A^3 = 0, then (I + A + A^2/2)^{-1} = I − A + A^2/2; thus matrix 2A^2 + A + I is invertible with explicit inverse (1/4)A^2 − (1/2)A + I as shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use complex numbers and z + 1/z transforms for symmetric systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce complex variable z = u + iv (or use u+iv and its conjugate) to reduce symmetric/difficult real systems to algebraic equations in z and 1/z, then solve quadratics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: after substitutions √x = u, √y = v, form z = u + iv so that z + 1/z equals a known complex constant; solve quadratic for z and recover x,y.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count solutions by degree/size bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Use degree considerations (e.g., total degree of polynomial system) to bound the number of solutions and confirm completeness after finding that many solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: cubic system in three variables has at most 3^3 =27 solutions; after finding 27 explicit ones via trig substitutions, conclude the list is complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive periodicity by defining difference functions + boundedness argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Define auxiliary difference functions (e.g., g(x)=f(x+α)−f(x)), use given functional relations to show these have smaller periods, then use boundedness to conclude linear growth terms vanish and deduce periodicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IMOs/shortlisted problems: define g and h with fractional shifts (like 1/6,1/7) to show h(x) is 0 because boundedness would otherwise give unbounded kh(x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hermite/floor-function identities via periodicity arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove identities involving greatest-integer functions by defining a periodic function from the difference and showing it is identically zero because its period and values on a fundamental interval force it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: show ⌊x⌋ + ⌊(x+1)/n⌋ + ... + ⌊(x+n−1)/n⌋ = ⌊nx⌋ by defining f(x) equal to the difference and checking periodicity and vanishing on [0,1/n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abel summation formula (discrete integration by parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the identity a1b1 + ... + anbn = (a1−a2)b1 + (a2−a3)(b1+b2) + ... + an(b1+...+bn) to transform sums into weighted partial sums, analogous to integration by parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply to polygonal complex-coordinate sums or to transform sums where coefficients form a decreasing sequence; used to show nonvanishing of certain complex sums and to derive inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use triangle inequality on unit complex factors to show nonvanishing
rubrics_metrics.description: When summing powers of a unit complex number weighted by positive decreasing coefficients, multiply by (1−z) and apply triangle inequality to show the sum cannot be zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in polygonal-line problem with z = e^{i(π−α)} and lengths a1 > a2 > ... > an, write sum via Abel formula, multiply by 1−z and apply |.| inequalities to conclude P0 ≠ Pn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telescoping trick for rational-function sums/products
rubrics_metrics.description: Find algebraic rearrangements that express terms as differences (or ratios) of consecutive terms so the whole sum/product collapses, e.g., k!·k = (k+1)! − k!.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: write k!·k as (k+1)! − k! to compute ∑ k!·k; or decompose rational factors to get telescoping cancellation in products and sums.
